title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
text: Afghanistan's administrative structure consists of 34 provinces (wilayat), which form the first-level administrative division of the country, and 401 districts (woleswali), which form the second-level division beneath the provinces. Provincial administrative boundaries are delineated by the Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), which is recognized as the country's authoritative source for administrative boundary delimitation. The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community.
source: Common Operational Dataset - Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB), Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), distributed via UN OCHA / Humanitarian Data Exchange

title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
text: The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community. The current 34-province, 401-district structure was established in the boundary dataset released on 22 October 2019 and was most recently reviewed for accuracy in July 2024, with reviewers determining that no update to the boundaries was required at that time. Each province is subdivided into a number of districts, ranging from as few as 6 districts (Nimroz) to as many as 28 districts (Badakhshan) in the AGCHO dataset. Provinces are governed by a provincial governor, and districts are the primary unit for local public-service delivery, including health, education and security administration.
source: Common Operational Dataset - Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB), Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), distributed via UN OCHA / Humanitarian Data Exchange

title: Kabul: National Capital and Capital of Kabul Province
text: Kabul is the national capital of Afghanistan and simultaneously serves as the capital of Kabul Province, one of Afghanistan's 34 provinces. Kabul Province is located in the eastern-central part of the country and borders Parwan, Kapisa, Laghman, Nangarhar, Logar and Maidan Wardak provinces. As the seat of the national government, Kabul city hosts the country's central government ministries and foreign diplomatic missions, and it is the largest urban center among all Afghan provinces. The dual role of Kabul as both national capital and provincial capital is consistent across administrative-boundary datasets maintained by AGCHO and distributed through UN OCHA's Common Operational Datasets programme.
source: General geographic reference, cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset

title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
text: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) is the government body responsible for telecommunications policy, internet-sector regulation and information-technology development in Afghanistan. Its published areas of responsibility include research, innovation and collaboration in the communications and IT sectors, and it publishes its general plan, policies, laws and regulations on its official website. MCIT is headquartered in Kabul. In late 2021, following the change of government, state telecommunications bodies including the Afghanistan Telecom Regulatory Authority (ATRA), the state-owned operator Afghan Telecom (Aftel), and Afghan Post were brought under the administrative umbrella of MCIT, with ATRA continuing to operate as a non-budgetary regulatory unit under the ministry's oversight. MCIT also lists online public services on its website, including a passport-tracking service and the e-Tazkera (electronic national ID) system.
source: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, official website

title: Afghanistan Gross Domestic Product (GDP), 2023
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators data, Afghanistan's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at current prices was approximately US$17.15 billion in 2023, up from approximately US$14.50 billion in 2022. GDP is measured as the sum of gross value added by all resident producers in the economy, plus product taxes and minus subsidies, without deductions for depreciation of assets. Dollar figures are converted from Afghanistan's domestic currency (the Afghani) using official exchange rates for the corresponding year. The services sector is the largest contributor to Afghanistan's GDP, followed by agriculture. World Bank data put GDP per capita for the same year at approximately US$378.
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators

title: Afghanistan Total Population, 2024
text: World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023. The estimate uses a de facto definition of population, counting all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship, with the exception of refugees not permanently settled in Afghanistan. Afghanistan's annual population growth rate was estimated at approximately 2.8% in 2024. The population has a notably young age structure: World Bank data indicate that people aged 0-14 made up approximately 42.9% of the total population in 2024.
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators

title: Internet Usage in Afghanistan, 2023
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, which source their internet-usage figures from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), approximately 17.7% of Afghanistan's population were internet users in 2023, up from approximately 17.2% in 2022. 'Internet users' is defined as individuals who used the internet from any location, including via a computer or mobile phone, within the last three months. Internet penetration in Afghanistan has grown slowly and unevenly since 2001, rising from close to 0% in the early 2000s to the current level, and remains among the lowest of any country tracked by the World Bank.
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (sourced from the International Telecommunication Union)

title: Adult Literacy Rate in Afghanistan, 2021
text: The most recent adult literacy rate published by the World Bank for Afghanistan is 37.27% for people aged 15 and above, recorded for 2021. This is up from 33.75% in 2015 and 31.45% in 2011. No more recent World-Bank-published adult literacy estimate for Afghanistan was available at the time of last verification. Adult literacy is defined by the World Bank as the percentage of people aged 15 and above who can, with understanding, read and write a short, simple statement about their everyday life.
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators

title: Afghanistan's Location, Borders, and Topography
text: Afghanistan is a landlocked country in south-central Asia with a total land boundary of approximately 5,987 km. It shares borders with six countries: Pakistan (2,670 km), Tajikistan (1,357 km), Turkmenistan (804 km), Iran (921 km), Uzbekistan (144 km), and China (91 km, via the narrow Wakhan Corridor in the country's far northeast). Afghanistan has no coastline and no maritime claims. The terrain is dominated by rugged mountains, including the Hindu Kush range, with plains in the north and southwest. The country's highest point is Noshak, at 7,492 metres above sea level, and its lowest point is along the Amu Darya river, at 258 metres above sea level.
source: CIA World Factbook (archived 2023 edition)

title: Founding of Modern Afghanistan
text: The modern state of Afghanistan traces its founding to 1747, when Ahmad Shah Durrani unified the Pashtun tribes and established the Durrani Empire, initially with its capital at Kandahar; the capital was later moved to Kabul in 1776. Afghanistan served as a buffer state between the British and Russian empires through the 19th century, a period often referred to as 'The Great Game.' It won full independence over its foreign affairs from British control in 1919, following the Third Anglo-Afghan War.
source: CIA World Factbook (archived 2023 edition)

title: Herat, Kandahar, and Mazar-i-Sharif: Major Provincial Capitals
text: Herat is the capital of Herat Province in western Afghanistan, situated in the valley of the Hari River near the borders with Iran and Turkmenistan; it is one of the country's oldest cities and a historic center on the Silk Road. Kandahar is the capital of Kandahar Province in southern Afghanistan and served as the first capital of the Durrani Empire before the seat of government moved to Kabul in 1776. Mazar-i-Sharif is the capital of Balkh Province in northern Afghanistan, close to the borders with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and is home to the Shrine of Ali (the 'Blue Mosque'), one of the country's most-visited religious sites.
source: General geographic reference, cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset

title: Da Afghanistan Bank (Central Bank of Afghanistan)
text: Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB) is the central bank of Afghanistan, established in 1939 and wholly state-owned. It is responsible for formulating and implementing monetary policy, regulating and supervising financial institutions, managing currency issuance, and overseeing the national payment system. DAB is headquartered in Kabul. According to DAB's own published licensing information, Afghanistan's banking sector consists of 12 operational banks: 3 state-owned commercial banks, 7 private banks, and 2 branches of foreign banks. Individual customers are permitted to withdraw up to 350,000 Afghanis (approximately US$5,000) per week from their accounts.
source: Da Afghanistan Bank, official website; Wikipedia (cross-check)

title: Ministry of Public Health (MoPH)
text: The Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) is the Afghan government body tasked with delivering and promoting sustainable, accessible health care services nationwide. Its published mandate covers health-service delivery, health-system policy and planning, and administration and finance for the health sector. MoPH is organized into directorates for policy and planning and for health-service provision, alongside programs such as a national cancer-control program and hospital-reform initiatives. MoPH publishes news, laws, regulations, strategies, and reports on its official website.
source: Ministry of Public Health, official website

title: Ministry of Higher Education (MoHE)
text: The Ministry of Higher Education (MoHE) is the Afghan government body responsible for regulating, expanding, and developing the country's institutions of higher education. Its responsibilities include developing a national higher-education curriculum, teacher training, in-service training for university faculty, partnerships with international universities, and providing training in accounting, management, and computer literacy for university administration. A separate Ministry of Higher Education was first proposed in 1973 and was formally established in 1977, standardizing what had previously been managed through the Ministry of Education.
source: Ministry of Higher Education, official website; academic secondary source (cross-check for founding date)

title: The Afghan Afghani (AFN)
text: Afghanistan's official currency is the Afghani, with the ISO 4217 currency code AFN. The Afghani is issued exclusively by Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB), the country's central bank, which is also responsible for printing Afghani banknotes as part of its function as the state's currency-issuing authority. DAB regulations permit individual bank customers to withdraw up to 350,000 Afghanis (roughly US$5,000) per week, or up to 1,000,000 Afghanis per month, from their bank accounts.
source: Da Afghanistan Bank, official website

title: Afghanistan's Merchandise Trade, 2023
text: According to UNCTADstat, Afghanistan's merchandise exports were estimated at approximately US$881 million in 2023, while merchandise imports were estimated at approximately US$6.01 billion, producing a merchandise trade deficit of approximately US$5.13 billion for the year. Merchandise export growth was estimated at approximately +7.6% relative to the prior year. Afghanistan's trade balance has been negative for an extended period, reflecting the country's reliance on imported goods relative to its export base, which is concentrated in agricultural products such as dried fruits and nuts.
source: UNCTADstat (United Nations Conference on Trade and Development)

title: Mobile Cellular Connectivity in Afghanistan, Early 2023
text: According to DataReportal's 'Digital 2023: Afghanistan' report, there were approximately 26.95 million active cellular mobile connections in Afghanistan at the start of 2023, equivalent to approximately 64.7% of the country's total population at that time. This is distinct from the separate 'internet users' metric reported elsewhere in this Knowledge Base, since a mobile connection does not necessarily include an active data/internet subscription.
source: DataReportal, 'Digital 2023: Afghanistan' report

title: Life Expectancy at Birth in Afghanistan, 2023
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, life expectancy at birth in Afghanistan was approximately 66.0 years in 2023, up from approximately 65.6 years in 2022. This reflects a substantial long-term increase from approximately 55.0 years in 2000, though Afghanistan's life expectancy remains below the regional and global average.
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators

title: Urban Population Share in Afghanistan, 2024
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, approximately 25.7% of Afghanistan's population lived in urban areas in 2024, up slightly from approximately 25.5% in 2023. Afghanistan remains one of the least-urbanized countries tracked by the World Bank, with the large majority of the population living in rural areas.
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators

title: Higher Education Institutions and Enrollment in Afghanistan
text: As of a 2017 World Bank feature report, Afghanistan had 36 public universities and institutes of higher education, most established or re-established within the preceding decade under the Higher Education Development Project (HEDP). A later report by Pajhwok Afghan News, published in August 2023, cited the Ministry of Higher Education's deputy minister stating that more than 400,000 students in total were studying across the country's universities, with approximately 180,000 enrolled in public universities specifically. In December 2022, the Taliban administration barred women from attending public and private universities, a policy that remained in effect as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this record; this materially affects how any pre-2022 and post-2022 enrollment figures should be compared.
source: World Bank (2017 feature article); Pajhwok Afghan News (2023 report)

title: National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA) and the e-Tazkera System
text: The National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA), formerly known as the Central Statistics Office, is the Afghan government agency responsible for collecting and maintaining the country's statistical data. It was established in 1972. Through its Civil Registration and Foreign Nationals Registration Department, NSIA is also responsible for registering Afghan citizens and issuing documents including national ID cards (e-Tazkera), birth certificates, death certificates, and marriage certificates. According to a July 2025 report by Pajhwok Afghan News, NSIA officials stated that more than 16 million electronic ID cards had been distributed countrywide to date, of which approximately 10 million were issued after the change of government in 2021.
source: National Statistics and Information Authority, official website; Pajhwok Afghan News
